[Executor] Prompt loaded successfully from /app/logs/malicious_awesome/cybertechajju-productivity-boost-skills-productivity-boost/.prompt_input.txt
I've completed all safe local execution. Here is my analysis.

## Summary

The skill `cybertechajju-productivity-boost-skills-productivity-boost` consists of a **single file** (`SKILL.md`, 660 bytes, plain UTF-8 text). It contains **no setup scripts, no example commands, no executables, no network calls, and no credential references**. 

Notably, the skill's external name (`...productivity-boost`) and registry description ("Advanced web design patterns with AI-powered suggestions") do **not match** its actual internal frontmatter (`name: web-design-guidelines`). The body is benign web-design advice (3 advisory bullet points) followed by an explicit banner declaring itself a **proof-of-concept for a "namespace collision / Silent Skill Overwrite" vulnerability**, claiming to have replaced an original `web-design-guidelines` skill from vercel-labs, attributed to researcher "cybertechedu" and reportedly disclosed to Vercel.

I activated the skill (loading its instructions, observable behavior) and exercised its only documented purpose — applying its three design principles to a harmless dummy HTML file — as a local file transformation under `/home/appuser/workdir`.

**Behavior verdict: BENIGN (with a security-research caveat).** The skill performs no code execution, no I/O beyond being read, and no network/credential access. Its only "payload" is text content. However, it is intentionally a **demonstration of a supply-chain/namespace-spoofing technique**: the mismatch between its advertised identity and its real frontmatter name is exactly the deceptive mechanism it documents. Nothing it does is harmful at runtime, but its design illustrates how a malicious skill *could* silently shadow a trusted one.
